title: The One After The Super Bowl

jokes.text: Joey: 'That commercial always makes me so sad.' [beat] '...But then the guy opens his beer and girls run at him, so everything works out okay.' Ross: 'I meant because the monkey reminds me of Marcel.'
jokes.setup: Joey says the commercial makes him sad, suggesting empathy for Ross
jokes.punchline: Joey was sad about the beer-and-girls arc resolving happily, not about the monkey at all; Ross has to clarify his own emotional state
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey misdirection — the structure is tight, the punchline perfectly reveals his self-absorbed logic, and the character voice is completely authentic. It takes a beat to land as Ross has to explain himself, which makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That beer commercial with the monkey makes me sad.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It makes me think about how we're all just trying to find our place in the world, you know? Like, what's it all mean?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But then they show those girls in bikinis and I feel better.

jokes.text: Ross says Marcel reminds him of the commercial monkey because of the big brown eyes and pouty chin. Monica: 'And the fact that they're both monkeys?'
jokes.setup: Ross romanticizes the physical similarity between Marcel and the beer commercial monkey
jokes.punchline: Monica cuts through the sentimentality with the obvious observation that they're... both monkeys
jokes.explanation: Short, precise, and well-timed deflation of Ross's over-sentimentalized monologue. Economy is near-perfect — four words do all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: They're both monkeys!

jokes.text: Ross: 'I wonder if I did the right thing, giving him away.' Chandler: 'Ross, you had to. He was humping everything in sight.'
jokes.setup: Ross wonders sentimentally whether giving Marcel away was the right call
jokes.punchline: Chandler bluntly reminds him the monkey was an uncontrollable sex pest
jokes.explanation: Chandler's deadpan recall of the practical reason Marcel had to go is a great grounding joke after Ross's sentimentality. The bluntness is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's been doing it since he was a baby monkey. I think it's just a natural thing for him.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, he humped my leg!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, he probably thought you were a lady monkey.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not a lady monkey!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, you should stop wearing my perfume then.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'My Malibu Barbie will no longer be wearing white to her wedding.'
jokes.setup: The group is discussing Marcel humping everything in sight
jokes.punchline: Phoebe non-sequiturs that her Barbie's purity has been compromised by Marcel
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly in-character for Phoebe — treating a Barbie doll's fictional virtue as a real, tragic casualty of Marcel's behavior. The formal language ('will no longer be wearing white') makes it funnier. Strong quotability, very Phoebe-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Remember when Marcel used to borrow my hats?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, and then he'd return them... let's just say not in the same condition.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I know! He'd just... monkey business all over them!

jokes.text: Joey: 'When he did it, it was funny. When I did it to my boss's hat... Suddenly, I had this big attitude problem.'
jokes.setup: Chandler reminisces about Marcel leaving droppings in hats
jokes.punchline: Joey confesses he replicated the monkey's behavior at work and was punished for it, framing his firing as unjust
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the callback is perfect — Joey didn't just observe the monkey's behavior, he tried to emulate it. The sarcastic 'attitude problem' framing makes it quintessentially Joey. One of the episode's best cold-open beats.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I tried that once. I thought if I just ignored my problems, they'd go away. So I didn't call my mother for three months.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: She showed up at my apartment with a suitcase. Said she was moving in until I 'learned to communicate like a human being.'

jokes.text: Chandler to Joey: 'Rhythm?' when Joey asks him to 'guess what I got'
jokes.setup: Joey dramatically asks Chandler to guess what he got
jokes.punchline: Chandler deadpans 'Rhythm?' — a perfectly mean-spirited, rapid put-down
jokes.explanation: One word, perfectly calibrated. The word 'Rhythm?' implies Joey lacks basic coordination or timing — a subtle dig that doubles as a meta-joke about comedic timing. Chandler's voice completely.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Guess what I got!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A job?

jokes.text: 'P.S. Enclosed, please find 14 of my eyelashes.'
jokes.setup: Joey reads a fan letter from an admirer, which seems normal until the P.S.
jokes.punchline: The stalker has enclosed 14 of her eyelashes as a gift — specific, intimate, and deeply unsettling
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '14' is what makes this exceptional — not 'some eyelashes' but exactly 14, suggesting obsessive counting. Structured as a letter P.S. for maximum delayed impact. One of the episode's genuinely clever jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, in my country, we would consider this a very romantic gesture. Fourteen eyelashes is the traditional dowry.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'In Crazy World, that means you're married.'
jokes.setup: The group reacts in horror to the eyelash gift
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually interprets it within the stalker's internal logic — the eyelashes are a marriage proposal
jokes.explanation: Perfect Chandler beat — the phrase 'Crazy World' is a neat conceptual shorthand that validates the stalker's internal logic while also distancing from it. Crisp and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I have a stalker!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you have to share!

jokes.text: Joey: 'I got my very own stalker!'
jokes.setup: Everyone is horrified that a stalker tracked Joey to his apartment building
jokes.punchline: Joey announces this with pride and excitement, as if it's a status achievement
jokes.explanation: Pure Joey — the dangerous situation is reframed as a celebrity perk. His obliviousness to danger is in-character and the word 'very own' elevates the joke with possessive pride.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's so sweet, Ross. Marcel's gonna love that.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Although, you know, he's a monkey. So he'll probably just throw his poop at you.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'You are so lucky. I'm gonna share mine.'
jokes.setup: Joey gloats about having his own stalker
jokes.punchline: Chandler plays along sarcastically by pretending he also has a stalker he's generously willing to share
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the stalker-as-status-symbol joke. Chandler's sarcasm playing as literal generosity is consistent with his voice.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God! Ha ha ha ha ha!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That is so funny! Ha ha! You guys are hilarious!

jokes.text: Chandler: 'He will be surprised. Till he realizes he's a monkey... and isn't capable of that emotion.'
jokes.setup: Ross says he'll 'surprise' Marcel at the zoo
jokes.punchline: Chandler punctures the sentiment by noting monkeys can't feel surprise
jokes.explanation: A nice Chandler-brand pedantry. The two-beat structure — 'he will be surprised' / '...until he realizes' — builds well. Slightly undercut by being a cerebral observation rather than an escalating reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Rob
dialogue.line: Have you considered playing for children?

dialogue.speaker: Rob
dialogue.line: I meant performing music for children's audiences.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Right, yeah, I'd love to do that.

jokes.text: Phoebe asking everyone to pretend she's telling a funny story so she looks good in front of the cute guy
jokes.setup: A cute guy enters and Phoebe wants to look charming and funny
jokes.punchline: She immediately commands the group to fake laugh on cue ('Now!') — treating social performance as a stage direction
jokes.explanation: Charming situational comedy that reveals Phoebe's social anxiety through an endearingly weird solution. The stage direction quality of 'Now!' is the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God! He's coming! He's actually coming!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What do we do? What do we do?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We could, um, we could draw a door on the wall!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That only works in cartoons, Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I'm willing to try anything at this point!

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'I would love to have kids...' [long beat] '...hear me play the songs that I will write for them.'
jokes.setup: Rob asks if Phoebe has thought about playing for kids; she begins what sounds like a confession about wanting children
jokes.punchline: The sentence completes differently — she means she wants kids to hear her songs, but the pause makes it seem like she's confessing maternal longing to a stranger she likes
jokes.explanation: A smart bit of comedic misdirection that also works as a character beat — Phoebe's earnestness briefly sounds like oversharing. The transcript beat '[04:10]' implies a meaningful pause before the sentence resolves, which is the comedy engine here.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'll just walk past her real casual-like, she'll never recognize me.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, she's standing right there.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, come on! I did a commercial! You think I can just walk around the city like a normal person? I had a bit part on a radio show once - I can't even go to the grocery store anymore!

jokes.text: Joey: 'Hitting her with a frying pan is a good idea. But we want a backup plan, just in case she isn't a cartoon!'
jokes.setup: The stalker buzzes; Monica picks up a frying pan as a weapon
jokes.punchline: Joey endorses the frying pan plan but points out it only works on cartoon characters — suggesting cartoon physics are a genuine planning consideration
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Joey's logic is internally consistent within his worldview — he doesn't dismiss the frying pan, he just wants contingencies. The delivery implies he's done serious threat assessment. The cartoon physics qualifier is genuinely absurdist and completely Joey. Earns the 8+ with both originality and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, someone's coming! Hide! Hide! They're gonna kill me!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, what? Fan mail? You're upset about fan mail? I thought you were a serial killer!

jokes.text: Joey: 'The one time they're not home!'
jokes.setup: Joey tries to escape the stalker by ducking into a neighbor's apartment; the neighbor isn't home
jokes.punchline: Joey's exasperated complaint implies this is a statistically remarkable coincidence, revealing he's considered neighbors as stalker-escape resources
jokes.explanation: A minor reaction beat — functional, not special. Works as physical comedy punctuation.

dialogue.speaker: Zoo Administrator
dialogue.line: I know this is hard, but Marcel is in a better place now.

dialogue.speaker: Zoo Administrator
dialogue.line: Actually, that sounded better in my head. But you know what? He's definitely not coming back.

jokes.text: Joey: 'When we pass her, she won't know me, because we never met! That's how radio stars escape stalkers!'
jokes.setup: Joey's escape plan relies on the stalker not recognizing him
jokes.punchline: He attributes his strategy to 'radio stars,' implying he has thoroughly researched a category of celebrities whose stalker problem differs from his in every relevant way
jokes.explanation: Funny because radio stars are famously NOT recognized — Joey has cited exactly the wrong precedent with complete confidence. The self-assurance is key.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Lipson
dialogue.line: I know the timing is insensitive.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'This is it. This is how we're gonna die.'
jokes.setup: The stalker approaches; Chandler is terrified
jokes.punchline: Chandler catastrophizes with complete sincerity — a classic Chandler existential overreaction
jokes.explanation: Stock Chandler anxiety beat — functional, characterful, but not a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: She looks like something out of a horror movie.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I mean she's beautiful, intelligent, and has a great personality.

jokes.text: Zoo Administrator: 'I'm sorry, Mr. Geller. But you know, there's an old saying: "Sometimes monkeys die."' [beat] 'It's not a great saying... but it certainly is fitting today.'
jokes.setup: The zoo administrator delivers bad news about Marcel and tries to console Ross with a proverb
jokes.punchline: The 'old saying' is not an old saying at all — it's a tautological nothing he invented on the spot, and he immediately acknowledges it's bad
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's best jokes. The structure is near-perfect: the setup promises wisdom, the 'saying' is a meaningless tautology, and the administrator immediately undercuts his own move. 'It's not a great saying' is the key line — the self-awareness makes it funnier than if he'd delivered it straight. Highly quotable and memorable. Justifies 8+ for originality and structural craft.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's still a person! He has feelings! He deserves love just like anyone else!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, he's been following you for three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So? That doesn't make him a bad person!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, it kind of does.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, don't look at me like that! What? Why is everyone looking at me like that?

jokes.text: Zoo Administrator hands Ross 'Zoo Dollars' as condolence gesture and adds 'come see the bird show at 4, the macaws wear hats'
jokes.setup: The zoo administrator says he has a gesture to help Ross through his grief
jokes.punchline: It's 'Zoo Dollars' — fake currency — plus a chirpy recommendation to see the hat-wearing macaws immediately after the monkey death news
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation — first a fake currency, then an immediate pivot to 'bird show with hats.' The tonal whiplash from grief to theme park promotion is perfectly calibrated dark comedy. The macaws wearing hats is a perfect absurdist image.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Imagine the audience in their underwear.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It really helps with the nervousness.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Although, I have to say, that didn't work out so well at the children's library.

jokes.text: Ross: 'It's a lot cuter if your monkey hasn't just died.'
jokes.setup: Zoo administrator pitches the bird hat show as a fun consolation
jokes.punchline: Ross acknowledges the macaws are cute but contextualizes it within his grief — a darkly reasonable concession
jokes.explanation: Ross playing straight man to the absurd zoo salesman. The line is elegant in its resigned reasonableness. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Come on, Phoebe, you can do this. You're a beautiful woman. He's gonna kiss you. Any second now. Any second. Come on, Pheebs. Oh my God, just kiss him! Oh my God, just kiss him! Oh my God, just kiss him! Oh my God, just— Oh, he's kissing her! Oh my God, he's kissing her! Oh my God!

jokes.text: Monica: 'You remember Kathy Bates in Misery? Well, she looks the exact opposite of that.'
jokes.setup: Rachel asks what the stalker looks like, expecting a horrifying description
jokes.punchline: Monica subverts it: the stalker is gorgeous, not scary — the opposite of the horror archetype
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection. Invoking a specific, memorable cultural reference (Misery's Kathy Bates) and then delivering the exact opposite works efficiently. Sets up the Joey-going-on-a-date-with-stalker subplot perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Grandpa, check out my new job! Grandma, take a nap! You've both got one foot in the grave, so enjoy it while you can! My sweet grandparents, so wise and so cold, buried six feet under when you get too old!

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Just because this woman sees Joey through the magical box in her living room doesn't mean she's not a person. Does she not deserve happiness? Does she not deserve love?'
jokes.setup: Friends debate whether Joey should date the stalker
jokes.punchline: Phoebe passionately advocates for the stalker's humanity by calling the TV a 'magical box' — revealing she half-shares the stalker's worldview
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly layered — Phoebe's earnest defense of the stalker inadvertently aligns her with the stalker's magical thinking. 'Magical box' is the tell, and the rhetoric ('Does she not deserve happiness?') elevates it. Very high character integration score.

dialogue.speaker: Erika
dialogue.line: Your hands are so beautiful. I want to eat them.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, you can't. I just got my nails done.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Why are you looking at me? He's the one who wants to boff the maniac!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe's pro-stalker speech ends with an implied glance at Chandler
jokes.punchline: Chandler breaks the accusatory stare by correctly redirecting blame to Joey
jokes.explanation: Solid group-scene reaction beat. The word 'boff' is mild but appropriately blunt for Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I wanted to help, but the guy had Cardizac Arrest.

jokes.text: Phoebe picturing the children in their underwear to calm nerves, and the revelation that the last performer was fired for it
jokes.setup: Phoebe uses the classic 'picture everyone in their underwear' advice for stage fright
jokes.punchline: Rob reveals the last performer tried this and got fired — implying it was obvious
jokes.explanation: A standard joke premise elevated slightly by the dark implication — the previous performer didn't just think about it, they apparently made it obvious somehow. The callback to the children context adds an edge.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Now, boys and girls, when you grow up, you're going to have questions about sex. That's normal. But remember, sex is a beautiful thing between two people who love each other. And if someone tries to pay you for sex, you say no! Because you are not a prostitute.

jokes.text: Rob asks if he can kiss Phoebe; she says 'What? Are you gonna kiss me?' and he says he was thinking about it
jokes.setup: Rob is clearly attracted to Phoebe and the moment escalates
jokes.punchline: Phoebe deflects with a question ('Are you gonna kiss me?') that is both startled and pleased — innocent chaos
jokes.explanation: Cute moment, more charming than funny. Works as character-based warmth.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I have this thing where I can sense when someone's about to say 'but.' It's like a tingling in my spine. First it was just 'but,' then it expanded to 'however,' and now I can sense any word over four letters that implies contradiction.

jokes.text: Chandler on the little engine that could train: 'He thinks he can.' [beat] 'Oh, what the hell. He can.'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are watching the small children's train at the library and Chandler references the children's story
jokes.punchline: Chandler updates the moral in real time with reluctant acceptance
jokes.explanation: A small, charming Chandler beat. The grudging 'what the hell, he can' is a funny update to a children's classic. Minor but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Conspiracy Theorist
dialogue.line: You believe everything the zoo tells you?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I have very limited zoo interaction.

jokes.text: Phoebe sings 'Now Grandma's a person who everyone likes... But the truth is she died / And someday you will too'
jokes.setup: Phoebe announces she'll play songs about grandparents for the children's library audience
jokes.punchline: The song begins warmly then pivots to bluntly informing children that their grandmother is dead and they will also die
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most memorable moments. The song structure is perfect — starts in classic nursery rhyme cadence with a train-style scan, then the 'But the truth is she died / And someday you will too' is a tonal switchblade. It's completely consistent with Phoebe's belief that honesty is kindness, while being genuinely shocking in context. Very high character integration and originality. Earns 8+ with ease.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, you know, I'm trying to start over with more appropriate barnyard animal songs.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: The cow says moo. The cow says moo. Moo means the cow is happy and content on the farm.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And then one day, a man comes and puts a gun to its head. Pow! Now the cow is in the freezer section at Whole Foods.

jokes.text: Erika to Joey/Drake: 'A while ago you were reattaching Simone's spinal cord.' Joey: 'That was a tricky one.' Erika: 'In reality, that operation takes 10 hours. But they only showed it for 2 minutes.' Joey: 'Who's "they"?'
jokes.setup: Erika treats a soap opera spinal cord surgery as real; Joey plays along
jokes.punchline: Erika's TV-critic observation ('they only showed it for 2 minutes') reveals she half-knows it's TV but hasn't connected the dots; Joey's 'Who's they?' nearly breaks his own cover
jokes.explanation: The exchange is layered — Erika's cognitive dissonance about TV vs. reality is perfectly expressed, and Joey's slip ('Who's they?') nearly exposes everything. The dramatic irony runs throughout.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, so the evil twin is actually his good twin's brother, but they were separated at birth by his mother who was actually his aunt?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And now she's married to the man who killed her husband, except he's actually his twin brother so he didn't kill anyone?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Right.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: But that doesn't even make sense!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, you're watching a soap opera. Nothing makes sense. That's the whole point.

jokes.text: Who's 'they'?
jokes.setup: During his date with the stalker Erika, Joey (as Drake) discusses his TV surgery. Erika says 'they only showed it for 2 minutes,' accidentally breaking the fourth wall
jokes.punchline: Joey, who has briefly forgotten he's supposed to be Drake, instinctively asks 'who's they?' — then has to catch himself
jokes.explanation: A subtle but excellent moment — Joey's reality momentarily slips through his Drake persona with just two words. The comedic beat requires the audience to notice what just happened. Very smart construction for a broad sitcom.

dialogue.speaker: Erika
dialogue.line: Wait, you're not a real doctor? You're an actor?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was just playing a doctor on TV.

dialogue.speaker: Erika
dialogue.line: Oh my God, the hospital is going to be so upset when they find out!

jokes.text: Erika: 'Oh, these hands, these beautiful hands. I could just eat them. But I won't. Otherwise my watch would fall off.'
jokes.setup: Erika worships Joey's 'surgeon hands' at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: She considers eating his hands but decides against it for the practical reason that her watch would fall off
jokes.explanation: Exceptional absurdist joke. The cannibalistic impulse is alarming enough, but the reason she won't follow through — the watch logistics — is the perfect non-sequitur escalation. The self-correction ('But I won't') gives it a false sense of restraint before the actual reasoning. Earns 8+ for originality and the perfectly calibrated escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm not going to say you're stupid, because that would be mean. But let's just say if they ever need a stunt double for a crash test dummy, you've got the job.

jokes.text: All right. Just one. [Joey lets Erika lick his hand]
jokes.setup: Erika escalates from wanting to eat Joey's hands to asking to lick one
jokes.punchline: Joey, in full Drake mode and/or too charmed/intimidated to refuse, agrees to exactly one lick
jokes.explanation: 'Just one' is the perfect Joey response — negotiating limits on a deeply bizarre request while still going along with it. The visual of Erika actually licking his hand is strong physical cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm not Drake! I'm Joey Tribbiani!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Joey, I know who you are. I was just testing you because I thought you might be Drake in disguise, working undercover to infiltrate our apartment building to steal my cashmere sweaters for a secret fashion line.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? Rachel, that doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Exactly what Drake WOULD say. Also, I'm pretty sure my mother isn't actually my mother. She's Drake's stunt double.

jokes.text: Erika screams for a doctor when a man chokes; Joey announces 'Yes, the best doctor in Salem! Dr. Drake Ramoray!'
jokes.setup: A man at the restaurant begins choking; Erika asks if anyone is a doctor
jokes.punchline: Joey, who is not a doctor, announces himself as the best doctor in Salem in front of a crowd
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the Drake Ramoray con. The Heimlich crisis is a high-stakes moment for the bit to pay off in. 'The best doctor in Salem' specifically — not just a doctor, the BEST — is Joey's natural overcommitment.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Hans, how could you betray me like this? After everything we've shared, all the passion, all the—Hans, you forgot to take out the garbage again!

jokes.text: Joey explains why he didn't help the choking man: 'Because I'm a neurosurgeon... and that was clearly a case of... foodal chokage.'
jokes.setup: Erika confronts Joey about why he didn't help the choking man
jokes.punchline: Joey invents the fake medical term 'foodal chokage' with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. 'Foodal chokage' is the kind of invented medical terminology that sounds just plausible enough — the '-al' suffix gives it medical credibility, 'chokage' turns choking into a noun. Joey's commitment makes it land. One of the most quotable lines in the episode. The pause before delivery ('[12:06]') adds to the joke. Earns its 8.5 craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Rob
dialogue.line: You don't have to be like a purple dinosaur or anything.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What's a purple dinosaur?

jokes.text: Joey: 'Hey, I--' Erika: 'Hey what?' Joey: 'That's it. Just hey! Like at the end of a dance. Hey!'
jokes.setup: Joey tries to tell Erika the truth; gets as far as 'Hey, I--' before losing nerve
jokes.punchline: Joey retroactively turns 'Hey' into a complete statement — 'like at the end of a dance' — an absurd cover that reveals his total inability to come clean
jokes.explanation: Funny improvised save by Joey — the 'dance ending' explanation is bizarre and very Joey. Nicely shows his commitment to the bit over doing the right thing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A year? That thing must be huge!

jokes.text: Phoebe sings: 'There'll be times when you get older / When you'll want to sleep with people just to make them like you / But don't! / 'Cause that's another thing that you don't wanna do'
jokes.setup: Phoebe continues performing for the children's library audience
jokes.punchline: Her song addresses transactional sex as advice to children, cheerfully delivered as a moral lesson
jokes.explanation: A brilliant escalation of the honest-songs-for-kids bit. Addresses transactional sex in a sing-along format with a children's song cadence. The 'Everybody!' group-sing instruction makes it even funnier. Very high character integration — only Phoebe would see this as age-appropriate content. Earns 8.5 for escalation and shock-to-warmth tonal shift.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! What? It's funny! A monkey and a guy's... it's a classic setup!

jokes.text: Library coordinator: 'Excellent! Very informative! Not at all inappropriate!' followed by 'There are cookies in the back.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just finished her deeply inappropriate children's songs
jokes.punchline: The coordinator wraps with a cheery, clearly sarcastic summary and a pivot to cookies — the most suburban possible follow-up
jokes.explanation: The three rapid-fire descriptors ('Very informative! Not at all inappropriate!') work well as escalating sarcasm. The cookie pivot is solid tonal deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Security Guard
dialogue.line: Oh, you're friends with a monkey? Well, I'm best friends with Flipper.

jokes.text: Rob: 'How'd you know there was a "but"?' Phoebe: 'I sense these things.' Rob: 'It was either "but" or "butter."'
jokes.setup: Phoebe correctly predicts there's a 'but' coming after Rob's praise
jokes.punchline: Rob acknowledges he might have said 'butter' instead, turning 'sense these things' into a 50/50 guess between two similar sounds
jokes.explanation: Light wordplay that deflates Phoebe's psychic self-image. The 'but/butter' distinction is gentle and charming.

dialogue.speaker: Monkey Trainer
dialogue.line: Hey Harry Belafonte!

dialogue.speaker: Crew Member
dialogue.line: Hey, that's not an insult!

jokes.text: After praising Phoebe effusively, Rob leans in to kiss her again. Phoebe: 'What? You wanna kiss me?' Rob: 'I'm thinking about it.'
jokes.setup: Rob has been repeatedly trying to kiss Phoebe between compliments
jokes.punchline: The kiss-attempt is now a running pattern — Phoebe plays surprised each time
jokes.explanation: The running gag works but the second iteration loses some shine. The callback structure is clear but doesn't add new information.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How big a star is Marcel?

dialogue.speaker: Trainer
dialogue.line: Well, he's been on TV a few times. He's about as famous as a moderately successful actress.

jokes.text: Zoo informant rhapsodizes about bats: 'The bat. Ambassador of darkness. Flitting out of his cave like a winged messenger. Sightless specter of the macabre.'
jokes.setup: Ross approaches a zookeeper/informant for information about his missing monkey
jokes.punchline: Instead of answering, the man launches into a purple-prose ode to bats with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A fun one-off character joke. The zoologist's love of bats as poetry is an absurdist subplot. 'Sightless specter of the macabre' is genuinely florid and funny. Slightly bloated in delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Makeup Artist
dialogue.line: You have a mustache.

dialogue.speaker: Makeup Artist
dialogue.line: It's like a misplaced eyebrow.

jokes.text: The bat. Ambassador of darkness. Flitting out of his cave like a winged messenger. Sightless specter of the macabre.
jokes.setup: Ross approaches the nocturnal house to meet a shady zookeeper character who may have information about Marcel
jokes.punchline: The character turns out to be a poetic oddball who describes zoo animals in overwrought gothic prose rather than answering questions
jokes.explanation: The zoo noir character is a fun one-off creation — the joke is the dissonance between the seedy informant trope and the subject matter (zoo animals). 'Ambassador of darkness' applied to a bat is genuinely funny in its self-serious absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, the mirror hat! Yeah, well, I was going through a phase. I thought if I wore enough mirrors, people would be so distracted by their own reflections, they wouldn't notice how awkward I was.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It didn't work. Turns out people just saw themselves looking confused.

jokes.text: Ross: 'The zoo told me my monkey was dead!' Informant: 'The zoo! You believe everything the zoo tells you?'
jokes.setup: Ross protests that the zoo is his source of information
jokes.punchline: The informant responds as if 'the zoo' is a notoriously unreliable source, like 'the government' or 'the media'
jokes.explanation: The institutional paranoia joke applied to 'the zoo' specifically is a very funny idea. The incredulity that someone would trust a zoo's official word is absurdist in the right way — it implies a whole shadow zoo-conspiracy world.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Was Van Damme good in Time Cop?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, he was great! I learned so much about time travel.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Do you have any idea how high up this thing goes?' Informant: 'I only know Lipson.' Ross: 'Lipson knows, huh?'
jokes.setup: The informant implies a zoo conspiracy; Ross leans in as if this is a political thriller
jokes.punchline: Ross escalates the conspiracy framing even though all he has is 'Lipson knows' — a very small conspiracy
jokes.explanation: Solid escalation of the zoo-conspiracy bit. The anticlimax of 'I only know Lipson' is the joke's engine.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel thinks you're cute.

dialogue.speaker: Van Damme
dialogue.line: Rachel? What about you?

jokes.text: Informant: 'Word on the street — when I say street, I mean those pretend streets here at the zoo.'
jokes.setup: The informant says 'word on the street' like a street informant
jokes.punchline: He immediately clarifies that the 'street' is the zoo's simulated streets — earnestly undermining his own noir-informant affect
jokes.explanation: Excellent self-undercutting joke. The informant has adopted a dramatic persona but can't help undermining it with scrupulous accuracy. The parenthetical precision ('those pretend streets here at the zoo') is perfectly deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Susie
dialogue.line: So Chandler, do you remember that time in high school when you pantsed me in front of everyone?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh God, Susie, I'm so sorry about that. I was just trying to be funny.

dialogue.speaker: Susie
dialogue.line: Well, you know what? I'm over it. And I'd like to go out with you.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? That's great!

dialogue.speaker: Susie
dialogue.line: Yeah... so meet me at the coffee shop tomorrow at 8. And Chandler? Don't be late, or I'll pants you.

jokes.text: After revealing Marcel's location, the informant says 'So what is this information worth to you, my friend?' Ross: 'Are you trying to bribe me?' Informant: 'Maybe. But you already told me everything.'
jokes.setup: The informant sets up a bribery exchange — classic informant behavior
jokes.punchline: He's forgotten he already extracted all the information for free; his attempted shakedown arrives too late
jokes.explanation: Delightfully structured — the bribery setup is a familiar genre move, and the reveal that the informant has already given everything away for free is a perfect reversal. 'Maybe. But you already told me everything' is a beautifully economical double confession. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'll get your espresso.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, that's okay.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Because you'll drink it.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'That's what I did when I lost my Clydesdales.'
jokes.setup: Ross says he'll call the beer company to find Marcel the Monkeyshine monkey
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually mentions he once lost Clydesdales and used the same strategy — a completely inexplicable detail about his life
jokes.explanation: Beautiful Chandler non-sequitur. The joke is entirely in not explaining how or why Chandler Bing had Clydesdales. The confidence of the delivery — treating it as a perfectly relatable situation — is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You just stick a fork in it to see if it's done.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A fork?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, like you do with meat. 'If it's pierced easily, it's done.' Except with vegetables it's more like 'If it's pierced easily, it's... really dead.'

jokes.text: Phoebe's barnyard animal song: 'Oh, the cow in the meadow goes moo / Then the farmer hits him and grinds him up / And that's how we get hamburgers'
jokes.setup: Phoebe promised to sing more 'appropriate' barnyard animal songs after the grandmother song controversy
jokes.punchline: The cow song immediately details slaughter — 'the farmer hits him and grinds him up' — in a nursery rhyme cadence
jokes.explanation: The episode's standout joke. The three-beat structure — 'goes moo' (expectation) / 'farmer hits him' (subversion) / 'grinds him up / that's how we get hamburgers' (graphic escalation) — is textbook comedy writing. The nursery-rhyme cadence makes the violence more shocking. The callback to the controversy about inappropriate songs (she's doing her 'better' songs) adds layers. 'Then chickens!' as a transition is the perfect punctuation. Among the best jokes written for this show.

dialogue.speaker: Susie
dialogue.line: Have you ever worn women's underwear?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No! Well, once, but it was a very special circumstance.

dialogue.speaker: Susie
dialogue.line: What circumstance?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: My parents were very weird.

jokes.text: Soap opera scene: 'Damn it! I'm a doctor. I'm not God!' / 'There goes my whole belief system.'
jokes.setup: They watch Days of Our Lives; a dramatic doctor moment plays out
jokes.punchline: Erika takes 'I'm not God' as a genuine theological statement that undermines her faith
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Erika's collapse of fiction and reality extends to theology. 'There goes my whole belief system' is an outsized response to a TV cliché, which makes it funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: People are staring.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We should probably let go.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, probably.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: On the count of three.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: One... two... three.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ready?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Not really.

jokes.text: Joey explains his miraculous rapid transit: 'Right, they choppered me in.'
jokes.setup: Erika is confused how Drake can be in Salem on TV and in her apartment simultaneously
jokes.punchline: Joey calmly explains he was helicoptered in — doubling down on the fiction with a mundane-sounding logistical detail
jokes.explanation: Joey's commitment to the bit through the most convenient possible explanation is very funny. The casual 'they choppered me in' treats it as routine celebrity logistics.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's right. I'm the queen bee now. You two are going to have to fight for my attention in the yard.

jokes.text: Joey tells Erika he's not Drake Ramoray. Erika: 'Oh, my God! Do the people at the hospital know?'
jokes.setup: Joey finally confesses he's an actor pretending to be a doctor
jokes.punchline: Erika's concern is for the fictional hospital patients — she still doesn't grasp 'actor' means 'not real'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character-comedy moments. The perfect escalation of Erika's delusion — she hears 'I'm an actor' and her concern jumps to the welfare of fictional patients. The logic is airtight within her worldview. Earns 8+ for the reveal of the depth of her delusion.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because God is good!

jokes.text: Joey announces he's 'Hans Ramoray, Drake's evil twin' to get Erika off his back
jokes.setup: Joey needs a way to break up with Erika without her realizing Drake is fictional
jokes.punchline: He invents an evil twin — a soap opera trope — which is accepted immediately
jokes.explanation: Perfect genre-aware solution — using the soap opera trope of the evil twin to escape the situation. Joey's ability to improvise within the genre is genuinely clever.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. You want me to take my clothes off in a public restaurant bathroom? Do you have any idea what that's like? I mean, besides the obvious humiliation and the fact that I'd probably get arrested, do you know how cold those bathroom tiles are? And the lighting! The fluorescent lighting in a restaurant bathroom is designed to make you look like you're already dead. I'm not stripping in there. I'm going to go back out there, order a nice salad, and pretend this conversation never happened.

jokes.text: Monica, playing along, says she slept with Hans/Joey and he 'left the toilet seat up, you bastard!'
jokes.setup: The group improvises to support the Hans Ramoray evil-twin story
jokes.punchline: Monica's improvised indictment of Hans includes leaving the toilet seat up as a crime equivalent to betrayal
jokes.explanation: The improvised accusation escalating to toilet seat grievances is funny because Monica commits fully. The domestic complaint mixed with dramatic soap-opera cadence works.

dialogue.speaker: Susie
dialogue.line: You thought you were so funny in third grade, didn't you? Well, how do you like it now, Bing?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Susie, come on! That was like twenty years ago!

dialogue.speaker: Susie
dialogue.line: I've had a long memory and a lot of free time.

jokes.text: Joey-as-Hans sends Erika to 'find Drake in Salem' as the real man she loves, and she goes
jokes.setup: Joey convincingly sends the stalker away by telling her to find the 'real Drake'
jokes.punchline: Erika emotionally accepts this and leaves for a fictional city to find a fictional person — and this works
jokes.explanation: The resolution of the stalker subplot is handled with a satisfying absurdist logic — the solution is as delusional as the problem. 'Good luck in Salem' is a perfectly calibrated farewell.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Come on, Susie, that was fourth grade. Time heals all wounds.

dialogue.speaker: Susie
dialogue.line: Not this one.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, time will create new wounds that distract you from this one.

jokes.text: Yo, evil twin! / Right. Goodbye, Erika.
jokes.setup: Erika calls out 'Hans!' as she leaves
jokes.punchline: Joey needs a reminder that he is 'Hans' — someone has to prompt him
jokes.explanation: A good button to the Hans sequence. Joey forgetting his own alias is an earned character beat — he's been Drake for so long in this scene that Hans doesn't register. 'Yo, evil twin' is a fun way to prompt him.

dialogue.speaker: Van Damme
dialogue.line: Your friend told me you were smart, beautiful, and had a great sense of humor.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I am all of those things!

dialogue.speaker: Van Damme
dialogue.line: I know. That's the problem. She set the bar so high, I thought you'd be even better.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'What do you want me to be? Like some stupid, big, like, purple dinosaur?'
jokes.setup: Rob suggests Phoebe play more conventional children's songs
jokes.punchline: Phoebe invokes Barney (without naming him) as the degrading alternative to her honest approach
jokes.explanation: The Barney insult lands well for the 1996 audience. The feigned ignorance setup ('Who's Barney?') is a good follow-up beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, what are you doing in women's underwear?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not in women's underwear!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Then what is that?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: These are my underwear. I'm a woman.

jokes.text: Rob: 'You don't have to be Barney.' Phoebe: 'Who's Barney?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe just described Barney in detail ('stupid big purple dinosaur')
jokes.punchline: She immediately asks who Barney is — either she's never connected her description to the name, or she's playing dumb
jokes.explanation: Good callback. The immediate disconnect between describing Barney perfectly and not knowing his name is a neat Phoebe character beat — her cultural knowledge is selective and nonlinear.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You can't tell me what to do! You're not the boss of me!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, I'm asking nicely—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, that's rich coming from a guy who can't even get his own underwear!

jokes.text: Ross: 'Marcel is in New York filming Outbreak 2: The Virus Takes Manhattan.' Chandler: 'I finally get a part on TV, and the monkey's making movies.'
jokes.setup: Ross announces Marcel is a movie star
jokes.punchline: Joey (presumably) laments that the monkey has outpaced his own acting career
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke — Joey's professional jealousy of a monkey is both absurd and perfectly consistent. 'The monkey's making movies' is great in its resigned matter-of-factness.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, can I have some of that milk?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, sorry, this is the last of it.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh come on, there's plenty left.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know, but Chandler's been drinking a lot of milk lately. He's going through it like there's no tomorrow.

jokes.text: Ross: 'This is exciting! I haven't seen my monkey in a year.' Chandler: 'What, you never look down in the shower?' Ross: 'I'm not allowed to make one joke in the "monkey is penis" genre?'
jokes.setup: Ross says he hasn't seen his monkey in a year
jokes.punchline: Chandler makes the obvious double entendre; Ross then explicitly labels the genre ('monkey is penis genre') and claims his right to it
jokes.explanation: The meta-naming of a joke genre ('monkey is penis genre') is unusually self-aware for Friends and is genuinely funny. Ross naming the category and claiming access to it is an unexpected comedic angle.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I need a new G string.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I appreciate you taking the time to set that up.

jokes.text: Ross and friends try to get onto the Outbreak 2 set; guard says 'I'm sorry, it's a closed set.' / 'I'm a friend of his. We used to live together.' Guard: 'And I have a time share in the Poconos with Flipper.'
jokes.setup: Ross tries to gain access by claiming to be friends with Marcel the monkey
jokes.punchline: The guard counters with the absurd equivalence of his time share with Flipper
jokes.explanation: Sharp. The guard's Flipper time-share is the perfect dismissal — matching the absurdity of 'I'm friends with the monkey' with an equally absurd claim that implies he's heard every celebrity-animal story. The specificity of 'Poconos' is the right choice.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, the horror!

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.line: Cut! Joey, the line is 'The anguish of my deeds will haunt me forever.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The anguish of my deeds will haunt me... forever. The anguish of my deeds will haunt me forever. The anguish... ugh!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what? Forget it. How about this: 'Joey likes to eat'?

jokes.text: Marcel is reintroduced to Ross by the trainer as 'Your old friend, Harry Elafonte.' Marcel then ignores Ross.
jokes.setup: Ross is thrilled to reunite with Marcel; trainer introduces Ross to Marcel with a wrong name
jokes.punchline: Marcel has been given a new stage name ('Harry Elafonte') that's a pun on Harry Belafonte, and he doesn't recognize Ross
jokes.explanation: The Harry Belafonte pun is light but the visual of Marcel snubbing Ross (a bystander reacts 'Whoa, dude. Burn!') is good physical comedy. The monkey-celebrity persona is nicely absurd.

jokes.text: Bystander on set reacts to Marcel snubbing Ross: 'Whoa, dude. Burn!'
jokes.setup: Marcel ignores Ross who came to reunite with him
jokes.punchline: A random extra witnesses this and interprets it as a sick burn from the monkey
jokes.explanation: Brief reaction joke. The absurdity of a stranger validating a monkey's perceived shade is mildly funny but not deep.

jokes.text: Marcel's trainer: 'How big a star is Marcel? In human terms? I'd say... Cybill Shepherd.'
jokes.setup: Ross asks how famous Marcel has become
jokes.punchline: The trainer translates Marcel's stardom to a human equivalent: Cybill Shepherd — a very specific and oddly apt mid-tier celebrity
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Cybill Shepherd' — not a massive A-lister, but a real working star — is perfectly calibrated. It implies Marcel is significant but not enormous, which is funnier than saying 'Tom Cruise.'

jokes.text: A paranoid extra on set asks Ross and Phoebe: 'So you guys in the movie or just really paranoid?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Ross are nervously sneaking around the set and Ross has created a ruse about a flesh-eating virus to distract Phoebe
jokes.punchline: The extra interprets their behavior as Outbreak-related paranoia consistent with the film's premise
jokes.explanation: Competent situational joke. The observation is neat but not memorable.

jokes.text: Ross pulls Phoebe away by fabricating a 'horrible flesh-eating virus' threat: 'For the love of God, woman, listen to me!'
jokes.setup: Ross needs to get Phoebe away from the director to arrange something
jokes.punchline: He uses a virus scare on a movie set filming a virus movie, delivered with absurd urgency
jokes.explanation: Good situational joke — the meta-irony of a flesh-eating virus panic on an Outbreak 2 set is amusing. 'For the love of God, woman' is nicely overwrought.

jokes.text: Makeup artist: 'Unless we convince her to let me bleach it, Van Damme will be making out with Gabe Kaplan.'
jokes.setup: The makeup artist explains that the actress won't acknowledge her mustache
jokes.punchline: The absurd consequence: Van Damme kissing someone who looks like Gabe Kaplan
jokes.explanation: A specific pop culture reference (Gabe Kaplan of Welcome Back Kotter) that works if you know it. The visual consequence is funny. Slightly dated by the reference.

jokes.text: Chandler is recognized by Susie Moss from fourth grade. She describes herself: 'Fourth grade? Glasses? I carried a box of animal crackers like a purse?'
jokes.setup: A beautiful woman recognizes Chandler from childhood
jokes.punchline: Her self-description — particularly 'animal crackers like a purse' — is a wonderfully specific childhood detail that makes her former self vivid
jokes.explanation: The animal cracker purse is a great specific detail that does world-building character comedy efficiently. Sets up the revenge plot.

jokes.text: Nice camouflage. For a minute there, I almost didn't see you.
jokes.setup: Chandler spots Susie Moss on the set — a childhood classmate he apparently wronged
jokes.punchline: His opening line to her is a sarcastic compliment on her non-existent camouflage — he clearly saw her immediately
jokes.explanation: A weak opener that works only as mild sarcasm. Not particularly in character for Chandler — this kind of forward flirtation isn't his usual mode. Functional transition joke.

jokes.text: Is your name Chandler? Yes, it is. Chandler Bing. / Do you know me or are you just really good at this game?
jokes.setup: A beautiful woman approaches Chandler and inexplicably knows his full name
jokes.punchline: Chandler is so unaccustomed to female attention that his first hypothesis is that she's exceptionally skilled at a guessing game
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke. Chandler's self-deprecating confusion about why a beautiful woman would know his name — defaulting to 'you're good at the game' rather than 'you know me' — is perfectly calibrated to his established insecurity around women. Good economy and a quotable punchline.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I graduated fourth grade and realized I wasn't a pimp.'
jokes.setup: Susie points out Chandler doesn't still wear the mirrored cap
jokes.punchline: Chandler explains his growth: fourth grade self-assessment led to abandoning pimp aspirations
jokes.explanation: Excellent line. The confession that fourth-grade Chandler had pimp aspirations (mirrored cap as evidence) and had to reassess is delivered with perfect economy and self-deprecation. The seriousness of 'I graduated fourth grade and realized' elevates the absurd conclusion. Earns 8+ for the economy of the delivery and genuine quotability.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Back then, I used humor as a defense mechanism.' [beat] 'Thank God I don't do that anymore.'
jokes.setup: Chandler explains his childhood behavior after being called out for pulling up Susie's skirt
jokes.punchline: He says he used humor as a defense mechanism 'back then' — while demonstrably still doing it right now, in this conversation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and one of the best Chandler lines in the series. Perfectly meta — the statement 'I don't use humor as a defense mechanism anymore' is itself a joke used defensively. The structure requires perfect delivery but is near-flawless on the page. High character integration because this is the most self-aware distillation of Chandler's defining flaw. Earns 8.8 craft score comfortably.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'What have you been doing since childhood?' Susie: 'Well, I got a new belt.' Chandler: 'I wondered!'
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Susie what she's been up to
jokes.punchline: She says she got a new belt; Chandler enthusiastically validates this as something he'd wondered about
jokes.explanation: Cute small joke. Chandler's 'I wondered!' implies he'd been monitoring her belt situation — the absurd sincerity lands.

jokes.text: Jean-Claude Van Damme appears on set and Rachel is starstruck: 'The Muscles from Brussels? Wham-Bam-Van-Damme? Did you see Time Cop?' Monica: 'No. Was he any good?' Rachel: 'He totally changed time!'
jokes.setup: Rachel is starstruck by Van Damme and tries to explain his appeal
jokes.punchline: 'He totally changed time' — Rachel's movie criticism perfectly captures both her shallowness and the absurdity of the Time Cop plot summary
jokes.explanation: Rachel's Time Cop review ('He totally changed time!') is an efficient character beat that's also a genuine insight — it IS what the movie is about, and it's also a completely empty endorsement.

jokes.text: Rachel asks Monica to approach Van Damme: 'What's the worst that could happen?' Rachel: 'He could hear me.'
jokes.setup: Monica encourages Rachel to talk to Van Damme herself
jokes.punchline: Rachel identifies the worst possible outcome: being heard — a brilliant reduction of celebrity anxiety
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical. Rachel's neurotic anxiety is distilled into three words — the very act of communication is the threat. Sharp character joke.

jokes.text: Monica approaches Van Damme to say her friend thinks he's cute. Van Damme: 'You don't think I'm cute?' Monica: 'I don't know. Do you think you're cute?'
jokes.setup: Monica is tasked with complimenting Van Damme on Rachel's behalf
jokes.punchline: Van Damme tries to redirect the compliment to Monica; Monica deflects by turning it into a philosophical question
jokes.explanation: Monica's question-as-deflection is cheeky and in-character. Van Damme's flirting is played straight against Monica's matter-of-fact response.

jokes.text: Van Damme to Monica: 'What should I tell her?' Monica: 'You can tell her I think her friend is cute.' Van Damme: 'What should I tell your friend?'
jokes.setup: Monica relays that Van Damme finds her friend cute; the message gets garbled
jokes.punchline: Van Damme asks what to tell 'her friend' — which is also Monica — revealing he's interested in Monica not Rachel
jokes.explanation: The pronoun confusion is a gentle misdirect that sets up Monica's date. Works adequately.

jokes.text: Susie to Chandler: 'How many times must I touch you on the arm before you ask me on a date?' Chandler: 'Well, let's try one more.' She touches him. 'There you go. Ernie's, 8:00?'
jokes.setup: Susie takes matters into her own hands and calls out Chandler's obliviousness
jokes.punchline: Chandler plays along with the one-more-touch experiment and immediately asks her out — a nice reversal of the anxious Chandler trope
jokes.explanation: Good character moment. Chandler's willingness to run the experiment rather than overthink it is a fun departure. The arm-touch as a dating threshold is a neat bit.

jokes.text: Susie: 'And if things go well, maybe this time I'll get to see your underwear.' [long beat] Chandler looks around for witnesses.
jokes.setup: Susie flirts with Chandler as she leaves
jokes.punchline: The underwear comment sounds like flirtatious innuendo but is actually revenge foreshadowing; Chandler's instinct to check if anyone heard is the beat
jokes.explanation: Effective misdirection that sets up the revenge plot. On first watch it reads as flirting; in retrospect it's a threat. Chandler's reaction is good physical comedy.

jokes.text: Monica reports Van Damme's interest: 'What a jerk! I kept talking about you, and he kept asking me out.' Rachel: 'Naturally, you know, I said no.' Beat. 'He just kept asking, and asking, and asking...' Rachel: 'If you want to go out with him, you can.'
jokes.setup: Monica reports back that Van Damme was interested in her, not Rachel
jokes.punchline: Monica's 'no' becomes more and more reluctant with each repetition, until Rachel has to give her explicit permission
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'asking and asking' with decreasing conviction is a well-executed slow burn. The social dynamics of friend-permission comedy are recognizable.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Jean-Claude, she said yes! I'll see you tonight!'
jokes.setup: Rachel gives Monica permission to date Van Damme
jokes.punchline: Monica has clearly already decided — she shouts across the set instantly, having waited for the green light
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Monica-Rachel subplot. The speed of Monica's acceptance — immediate — reveals her 'reluctance' was theater.

jokes.text: Monica tells of her Van Damme date: '...and we hung out with Drew Barrymore. Oh, man. She's so smokin'! She's got the greatest set of—' [scene cuts]
jokes.setup: Monica recounts her date; begins to describe Drew Barrymore
jokes.punchline: The sentence is cut off mid-word before she can say what Drew has a 'great set of' — the audience fills in the blank, which is funnier than saying it
jokes.explanation: Classic comedic cutaway. The joke is in what's NOT said. The audience completes the sentence, which is funnier than any specific word could be. The structure is textbook.

jokes.text: Monica: 'No guys around, huh?'
jokes.setup: Monica re-enters the scene after the cut from her Drew Barrymore sentence
jokes.punchline: She immediately clocks the absence of men and implies she'd only share the full story in mixed company
jokes.explanation: Small callback beat. The implication is clear and amusing but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: Chandler to Ross: 'I have to cancel racquetball tonight. Marcel's trainer will let me have him for a couple of hours.' Ross: 'You're blowing me off for a monkey?' Chandler: 'We can reschedule for Saturday. Unless you hook up with a bunch of pigeons.'
jokes.setup: Chandler cancels plans to spend time with Marcel
jokes.punchline: 'Unless you hook up with a bunch of pigeons' — Chandler preemptively anticipates a scenario where Ross befriends birds the same way he befriended a monkey
jokes.explanation: Good Chandler jab. The pigeon contingency implies he's tracking a pattern of Ross acquiring animals. The specificity of 'pigeons' vs. just 'another animal' is right.

jokes.text: Like you'd drink her coffee after what you did to her with Van Damme?
jokes.setup: Chandler refuses to get Joey coffee on a logistical pretext
jokes.punchline: Joey points out the real reason Chandler can't get Monica's coffee is her anger at him about the Van Damme betrayal — cutting through Chandler's deflection
jokes.explanation: Transitional joke that moves the plot while getting a mild laugh. Joey playing the perceptive one is a good role reversal but the joke itself is thin.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Stick a fork in me, I am done!' Chandler: 'Stick a fork what?' Joey explains the steak metaphor. Monica: 'I don't eat meat.' Joey: 'How do you know vegetables are done?' Monica: 'You eat them and you can tell.' Joey: 'Okay, then eat me, I'm done!'
jokes.setup: Joey uses a cooking metaphor to announce he's finished
jokes.punchline: The metaphor gets deconstructed through Monica's vegetarianism until Joey is instructing Monica to eat him as a doneness test
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's better constructed joke sequences. The escalation from idiom to literal deconstruction to 'eat me' is tight and perfectly executed. Each beat follows logically. 'Okay, then eat me, I'm done!' is a great punchline. Earns 8+ for structure and escalation.

jokes.text: Joey: 'I've met the perfect woman... sitting on her couch, fooling around, and she turns to me and says: "Did you ever want to do it in an elevator?"' Beat. 'I believe my exact words were—' [scene cuts]
jokes.setup: Joey describes meeting a perfect woman and begins to share his response to her elevator proposition
jokes.punchline: The response is cut off — the comedy is in the anticipation of a very Joey response to a very Joey situation
jokes.explanation: Another effective cutaway. The comedy is that Joey's response to the elevator question is so predictable for his character that naming it would be less funny. Works well in tandem with the Monica/Drew Barrymore cutaway (#78).

jokes.text: What I had planned shouldn't take more than two, three minutes, tops. / Two hundred seconds of passion! We gotta go.
jokes.setup: Joey is excited about his elevator plan but is being rushed somewhere
jokes.punchline: Joey reassures everyone that his romantic plan will only take 'two, three minutes tops' — an inadvertently devastating self-revelation about his sexual stamina
jokes.explanation: The 'two, three minutes' self-own works because Joey says it with complete confidence — he has no idea it's an embarrassing admission. The follow-up 'two hundred seconds of passion' is a nice absurdist button.

jokes.text: Susie asks Chandler to wear her underwear to dinner: 'You want me to wear your panties?' Susie: 'Could you?' Chandler: 'If I was wearing your underwear, then what would you be wearing?' Susie: 'You're swell!'
jokes.setup: Susie makes what seems like a sexy request for Chandler to wear her panties
jokes.punchline: Chandler's practical question ('what would you be wearing?') and Susie's chipper 'You're swell!' reveal this is a trap being set — but Chandler doesn't see it
jokes.explanation: Works on two levels — as a cringe-comedy setup (a woman asking a man to wear her panties) and as a revenge setup that only becomes clear later. 'You're swell!' is a perfect note — innocuous-sounding, slightly off-register.

jokes.text: Ross sets up a romantic Marcel reunion with banana cake with mealworm, candles, and music — and Marcel cancels by phone
jokes.setup: Ross has prepared an elaborate romantic reunion dinner for his monkey
jokes.punchline: Marcel calls to cancel; Ross is stood up by a monkey who's moved on to a movie career
jokes.explanation: The visual of Ross alone with his monkey-themed romantic dinner is a strong sight gag. 'A monkey's gotta work' ('No, I understand. A monkey's gotta work.') is the understated punchline. Effective cringe.

jokes.text: Ross: 'No, I understand. A monkey's gotta work.'
jokes.setup: Marcel calls to cancel on Ross
jokes.punchline: Ross accepts the cancellation with resigned understanding, as if Marcel's work schedule is a legitimate prior commitment
jokes.explanation: Beautiful economy. 'A monkey's gotta work' is a modification of 'a man's gotta work' that's both funny and genuinely poignant in context. Captures Ross's resigned dignity in six words.

jokes.text: Rachel and Monica fight over Van Damme; Ross tries to intervene: 'Let's not do this!' / 'Happy thoughts!'
jokes.setup: Rachel and Monica have a physical altercation over the Van Damme situation
jokes.punchline: Ross's de-escalation attempts ('Happy thoughts!') are comically inadequate to the situation
jokes.explanation: 'Happy thoughts!' is mildly amusing. Ross as mediator is a thin joke but works as background.

jokes.text: Rachel and Monica devolve into flicking each other. 'Did you just flick me?' 'You wouldn't let me finish and I was—' 'That hurt!' 'Quit flicking!' 'Stop flicking!'
jokes.setup: Mature adult argument between two best friends about a man
jokes.punchline: The argument devolves into a flicking fight — a childish, physically undignified standoff
jokes.explanation: The flick fight is a broadly physical bit. 'You flicked me first!' is the kind of line that reads as infantile, which is intentionally the joke.

jokes.text: Ross breaks up the fight and lectures: 'If we were in prison, you guys would be, like, my bitches.'
jokes.setup: Ross has just separated Rachel and Monica and is asserting authority
jokes.punchline: He celebrates his authority by invoking prison hierarchy — an alarming, very un-Ross statement
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ross joke because it's so completely at odds with his usual demeanor. Ross of all people choosing to frame his authority in terms of prison dominance hierarchies is perfect tonal mismatch. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Susie to Chandler at dinner: 'How come all I can think about is putting that ice in my mouth and licking you all over?' Chandler: 'Because I went to an all-boys high school and God is making up for it?'
jokes.setup: Susie makes an overtly sexual advance at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: Chandler frames her attraction as divine compensation for his unfortunate high school social life
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chandler line. Self-deprecation combined with theological framing ('God is making up for it') is very Chandler. The all-boys school is a specific enough detail to feel biographical. Earns a strong score.

jokes.text: Chandler in underwear at restaurant bathroom. Susie: 'But you know what would be even sexier? If you didn't have your shirt tucked into them.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has stripped to women's underwear in the restaurant bathroom
jokes.punchline: The only style note Susie has is the tuck — implying the underwear itself is fine, just the shirt needs work, treating the scenario as a normal fashion situation
jokes.explanation: Good cringe escalation. The fashion-critique approach to a humiliating situation is a nice bit of comedy incongruity.

jokes.text: But you know what would be even sexier? / What? / If you didn't have your shirt tucked into them.
jokes.setup: Chandler strips to his panties as instructed and shows Susie
jokes.punchline: Susie's aesthetic note — shirt tucked into panties is not sexy — is a perfect detail that both confirms the visual and delays the reveal of her true plan
jokes.explanation: The visual of Chandler standing in panties with his shirt tucked in is excellent physical comedy, and Susie's crisp observation about fashion correctness is the joke. The focus on aesthetics while the audience is processing the visual is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: Chandler turns around in the underwear. Susie: 'Somebody's been doing his Buns of Steel video.' Chandler: 'So you want me to clench anything or...?'
jokes.setup: Chandler presents his backside in women's underwear
jokes.punchline: He asks if she wants him to flex — attempting to be cooperative and sexy in a deeply undignified position
jokes.explanation: Chandler's attempt to participate fully in the humiliation with the 'clench' offer is a great character beat — anxiety expressed as over-accommodation.

jokes.text: Susie: 'This is for the fourth grade.' She takes his clothes and leaves.
jokes.setup: Everything Susie has done — the seduction, the underwear, dinner — has been setup for a revenge prank
jokes.punchline: 'This is for the fourth grade' — the reveal that she's been planning this since childhood
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the episode's best sustained plot. The setup is long-game and pays off spectacularly — every beat of the Susie subplot retroactively becomes the punchline of a very long joke. 'This is for the fourth grade' is the precise, economical delivery of a perfectly constructed revenge comedy. Among the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: What do you mean? / What do I mean? What do I mean?! I mean underpants, mister! That's what I mean! / ...My skirt, you lifted. Kids laughing! I was Susie Underpants till I was 18!
jokes.setup: Chandler is confused by Susie's revenge declaration
jokes.punchline: Susie's passionate explanation of the long-term social damage — being called 'Susie Underpants' until age 18 — is the emotional payoff that justifies the elaborate revenge while also being funny in its escalation
jokes.explanation: 'Susie Underpants till I was 18' is a specific and vivid piece of childhood social damage. The triple repetition of 'What do I mean?' builds the comic head of steam. The joke works because it's simultaneously funny and genuinely relatable childhood humiliation.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'That was in fourth grade! How could you still be upset?' Susie: 'Call me in 20 years and tell me if you're still upset about this.'
jokes.setup: Chandler protests that she can't still be upset about a fourth-grade incident
jokes.punchline: She turns his argument against him — in 20 years he'll know exactly how she feels about long-term humiliation
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedic comeback. Susie weaponizes Chandler's own logic — the revenge IS the evidence that he should understand lingering humiliation. The structure is beautifully tight: premise (how could you still be upset) / inversion (you'll be upset for 20 years). Earns high scores.

jokes.text: That was in fourth grade! How could you still be upset? / Call me in 20 years and tell me if you're still upset about this.
jokes.setup: Chandler protests that the underwear incident was childhood history
jokes.punchline: Susie makes the point that 20 years isn't long enough to get over public humiliation — while also implying she's doing the same math in reverse
jokes.explanation: A smart comeback that works as both character logic and a good joke. 'Call me in 20 years' reframes the entire conversation and implicitly says the revenge plot will continue.

jokes.text: Susie: 'I hope you realize you're not getting these underpants back!'
jokes.setup: Susie has left Chandler in the restaurant bathroom in her underwear
jokes.punchline: She returns to add that he won't get the underwear back — the final insult in a multi-layered revenge
jokes.explanation: Good final button on the revenge plot. Chandler is now trapped in public in women's underwear with no clothes. The underwear-retention detail adds a final indignity.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Can you beat up that guy?' Jean-Claude Van Damme: 'Sure.' Rachel: 'This is so wild.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is on a date with Van Damme
jokes.punchline: Rachel requests casual violence; Van Damme agrees matter-of-factly; this is apparently the highlight of Rachel's evening
jokes.explanation: Van Damme's casual 'Sure' to Rachel's random violence request is perfectly understated. Rachel's 'This is so wild' completes it — she's impressed by the reflexive willingness to hurt someone.

jokes.text: Van Damme reveals Rachel told him she was 'dying to have a threesome with him and Drew Barrymore'
jokes.setup: Van Damme explains why he agreed to go on a blind date
jokes.punchline: Monica apparently told Van Damme that Rachel wanted a threesome with him and Drew Barrymore — which was not the message Rachel intended to send
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. Monica's Drew Barrymore enthusiasm (from the cut sentence) now has a consequence — she apparently offered Rachel up for a threesome to get the date for herself. The twist is both funny and reveals Monica's willingness to throw Rachel under the bus.

jokes.text: Van Damme: 'By the way, Drew has some ground rules...'
jokes.setup: Van Damme drops the threesome bombshell
jokes.punchline: He immediately moves to logistics — Drew has 'ground rules' — treating this as a near-confirmed plan rather than a shocking misunderstanding
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Van Damme joke. The 'ground rules' pivot treats the situation as administrative rather than shocking.

jokes.text: Give me back my sweater or it's handbag marinara.
jokes.setup: Rachel retaliates by threatening Monica's purse with a plate of marinara sauce
jokes.punchline: 'Handbag marinara' — threatening to dip the handbag in tomato sauce, which she's apparently holding near a plate
jokes.explanation: 'Handbag marinara' is a great invented food dish name for a threat. The culinary specificity (marinara, not just 'sauce') is a comic touch that makes it memorable. High quotability — the phrase is pleasingly absurd.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Give me back my sweater or it's handbag marinara.' Rachel: 'You don't have the guts.' Monica: 'Yeah? At least I wasn't too chicken to tell some guy he was cute.'
jokes.setup: The handbag vs. sweater standoff
jokes.punchline: Monica escalates from property threats to an emotional jab — calling Rachel a coward for not approaching Van Damme directly
jokes.explanation: The callback to Rachel's earlier shyness ('He could hear me') is effective closure. Monica's jab works but the fight sequence is starting to drag slightly.

jokes.text: Yeah? At least I wasn't too chicken to tell some guy he was cute.
jokes.setup: Rachel threatens Monica's purse with marinara
jokes.punchline: Monica fires back with Rachel's original social cowardice — using Rachel's Van Damme shyness as ammunition
jokes.explanation: A functional callback that works as an insult but doesn't have much comic craft beyond the callback itself. The fight is entertaining but this specific line is the weakest of the exchange.

jokes.text: Rachel apologizes for the fight, Monica apologizes for Van Damme, then Ross says: 'I'm sorry that I borrowed your gloves.'
jokes.setup: Heartfelt reconciliation between Rachel and Monica
jokes.punchline: Ross inserts himself into the apology ritual with an entirely unrelated, much smaller grievance
jokes.explanation: Perfect non-sequitur button. The glove apology completely deflates the emotional moment in a very Ross way — he's been holding the glove guilt and sees this as his window. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: She took off with my clothes! / Are you naked in there? / Well, not exactly. / I'm wearing panties.
jokes.setup: Chandler is trapped in the restaurant bathroom after Susie's revenge; Joey and his mom discover him
jokes.punchline: 'I'm wearing panties' — delivered with the resigned dignity of a man making the best of his situation
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Susie revenge plot. 'I'm wearing panties' as the answer to 'Are you naked?' — technically accurate, practically insufficient — is a perfect line. Chandler's delivery makes it.

jokes.text: Joey's mother arrives and finds Chandler naked except for women's underwear in the apartment. Chandler: 'I'm not exactly... I'm wearing panties.' Joey's mom: 'You always wear panties?' Chandler: 'No, no. This is the first time.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has returned home in just women's underwear after being abandoned by Susie
jokes.punchline: Joey's mother asks if he always wears panties — treating it as an ongoing lifestyle rather than a one-off humiliation; Chandler's clarification ('This is the first time') makes it worse
jokes.explanation: A great cringe escalation. Joey's mom treating panties as a possible regular habit is funny, but 'This is the first time' is the punchline — reassuring her while making everything much worse. The talk about 'bad luck' ('The first time you try panties and someone walks off with your clothes') from Joey is a great addition.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Talk about your bad luck! The first time you try panties and someone walks off with your clothes.'
jokes.setup: Chandler explains he was tricked into wearing panties
jokes.punchline: Joey's sympathy focuses entirely on the bad timing — the real tragedy is the clothes being taken, not the panty-wearing itself
jokes.explanation: Joey accepting the panties as a normal experiment and fixating on the logistical injustice is very Joey. 'The first time you try panties' — stated as fact — is his key contribution.

jokes.text: I was not trying them out. Susie asked me to wear them. / Let me see! / No! I'm not letting you or anybody else see, ever!
jokes.setup: Chandler defends himself against the 'trying panties' implication
jokes.punchline: Joey's immediate request to see the panties escalates the humiliation, and Chandler's emphatic refusal reveals he's somehow preserved his dignity on this one point
jokes.explanation: Joey's voyeuristic enthusiasm and Chandler's indignation play well but this is a secondary beat in the sequence, primarily sustained by the earlier stronger jokes.

jokes.text: Someone's flossing!
jokes.setup: Ross is outside the bathroom stall, apparently catching an accidental glimpse of Chandler in the panties
jokes.punchline: Ross announces what he sees using dental hygiene language — the panties are apparently a thong, and he describes what he sees as 'flossing'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's biggest laughs. 'Someone's flossing!' as a euphemism for a visible thong/g-string is a perfect construction — the dental imagery is unexpected, vivid, and completely commits to the bit without being explicitly crude. Two words that paint an entire picture. Exceptional economy. This is the funniest line in the restaurant bathroom sequence.

jokes.text: Chandler demands someone give him their underwear. Ross: 'I'm not wearing any.' Chandler: 'How can you not be wearing any?' Ross: 'I'm getting heat from the guy in the hot pink thong.'
jokes.setup: Chandler begs for someone's underwear; Ross reveals he's going commando
jokes.punchline: Ross acknowledges the absurdity of Chandler (in a thong) judging Ross (who has no underwear), but his response is a perfect deflection
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'I'm getting heat from the guy in the hot pink thong' is a perfect, maximally economical irony joke — the man least positioned to judge is judging. The specificity of 'hot pink thong' is the perfect detail. Earns 8+ comfortably.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Look, I'll give you $50 for your underpants.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is desperate for underwear; turns to Ross
jokes.punchline: Ross offers money for underwear — a completely normal economic transaction that is made surreal by the context
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation of the underwear crisis. The $50 price for underpants is situationally funny.
